title: runs/<run_id>/log.json — what an execution left behind (4.6, 4.6.9)
description: Not a card: the operator's record of one run. Derived from the artifact microscope_agent/src/operator.py already writes, not invented alongside it. Until this existed the file carried neither `card` nor `artifact`, so the collector skipped it and every check that names a run log -- 14, 15, 23, 37 -- had nothing to read and reported PENDING forever. The cost of that is specific: command provenance and the time base are the two things a run log exists to prove, and neither was being checked. The simulation side has no orchestrator and no device registry (4.6.8), so the fields that come from one are optional here; what is required is what both sides must answer for.

plan_id.description: the plan this run carried out. A run exists because a plan did (4.6) -- with one exception, settled 2026-09-24 (11-21): a PREPARATORY run carries null here, and then must carry `no_plan_because` and `approved_commands`, may dispatch nothing to the motion set, and produces no result card and no KB entry of its own. Its numbers reach the record only when a later plan cites its run_id as an input. Check 85 holds the parts a schema cannot: the motion set, and what cites the run. null is never a missing value: it is the statement that no plan governed this run, and the schema refuses it without the two fields that make that statement honest.

revision.description: the plan revision. An approval names (plan_id, revision), so a run that cannot say which revision it ran cannot be matched to one (6.1). null exactly when plan_id is null: a preparatory run has no plan and so no revision of one

approval.description: null id and kind is the honest state of a Tier 0-1 run: it needed no approval card, and saying so is different from failing to record one (6).

safety_policy_version.description: which envelope/safety.json was in force. Policy changes, and a run has to say which policy it ran under or the record cannot be read back later (2.1)

stop_criteria.description: ids of the monitors compiled from the plan. Stopping is a comparison against these, not a judgement (4.6.1)

t0_wall.description: wall-clock at t0, ISO 8601. Places the run in history; it does not order events

t0_mono.description: the monotonic origin every event offset is measured from (4.6.9)

backend.description: which backend ran it. mock is a first-class value: a plan runs unchanged on mock and on the engine, and that is the working definition of reproducibility (4.6.5)

registry_source.description: instrument side only: where the device registry was read from. Absent on the simulation side, which has no devices/ (4.6.8)

plan_path.description:
The plan file this run actually opened, repo-relative. `plan_id` and `revision` are copied from inside the card and agree with themselves whichever file was opened, so until 3eda760 nothing in a run record could distinguish 'ran revision 1 deliberately' from 'ran revision 1 because operator.py built the filename without a revision and could not see revision 2'. That second case ran the discarded experiment and finished green (tasks/009).

Optional, because three runs predate the field and P1 does not rewrite them; absent means the record cannot make that distinction, which is a fact about the record and not a defect in it. The operator now refuses a mismatch between the filename and the card's own `revision` at the one point where both are in hand, so this field and that refusal are two halves: the refusal stops the pair from lying, this says which file the pair came from.

no_plan_because.description: a preparatory run only: why no plan governed it, in words. Required with plan_id null and refused without it, so the field cannot be carried by a run that had a plan. The first one (2026-09-24) had none that fit: the only pre-measurement plan was 100x oil with software motion, and a 20x revision citing its axis ranges would have laundered them. A made-up plan_id to satisfy the old schema would have been a record claiming a plan that did not exist

approved_commands.description: a preparatory run only: the command list the person approved before any light, by path and sha256. It stands where a plan's scope approval would (11-21 condition 2). The path may lie outside the repository -- the first one sat beside its frames -- so check 85 verifies the hash when the file is readable from where the check runs and says so when it is not

approved_by.description: who approved, in words, as the approval was given

not_dispatched.description: a preparatory run only: that this run did not come through the plan dispatcher, and why, in words. Card 033 section 3b made this a condition of the first one, and that session wrote it here before this field existed; the field exists so the statement can stay where it was written rather than be moved to fit. Refused beside a plan_id, like the other two preparatory fields

event.description: One thing that happened, offset against the run's own t0.

t_mono.description: offset from t0_mono. Every event carries one, or the log cannot be put on a single timeline (check 37)

time_base.description: where this offset came from. software orders the log and nothing else: it carries OS scheduling jitter of milliseconds. A time a physical value depends on comes from a trigger counter or a device timestamp, and check 37 is what holds that line (4.6.9)

from.description: the plan.json field path this event was derived from. Commands are derived, never composed (4.6.1)

verification.description:
Whether the instrument was asked to confirm this command took effect. 4.6.6.1 rule 3 put its rule on this field and nothing carried it until 2026-09-20: the subsection says the run record carries `verification: none` for a channel that cannot be confirmed, and no such field existed. A rule written with nothing to hold it is the class counted most often that day.

`readback` means the channel's state was QUERIED AFTER the command and matched what was commanded. A return code is not a read-back: on the Tweez 300 a zero means the GUI accepted the text, and six distinct ways a command can be ignored all return zero (tweez300_reports_nothing_back, E3). An acknowledgement is `none`.

OPTIONAL ON PURPOSE, and check 66 rather than this schema is what requires it. Which actions need a read-back depends on reversibility, and reversibility lives on the plan's actions[] where a run log cannot see it -- an irreversible action requires one, a reversible one may legitimately go without. Leaving it out of `required` also keeps the two run logs written before the field existed valid, which is the honest reading: nothing asked them to record a read-back, so their silence is not a claim.

params.description: parameters as sent. Each one names the field it came from, so a number in a command can be traced to the card that justified it (check 14).

from.description: field path in plan.json, e.g. numbers[exposure_time]. A parameter that cannot name its origin does not go out

deletion.description:
A trajectory's positions were removed from this run directory (4.3.2, 2026-09-22). Deletion is the one operation that destroys the evidence for its own justification, so this records which DECLARED thing fired rather than why someone thought it should go.

It lives on a log event and not in trajectory_meta.json because that file has no schema: section 4 names it as an output and contracts/schemas/ does not hold it, so a deletion recorded there would be prose in an untyped file -- the defect this policy exists to avoid, inside the clause meant to preserve a record. The log is already an append-only record with a schema, and 13.1 put the watcher's output there for the same reason. trajectory_meta.json keeps saying what the trajectory WAS -- frames, steps, maximum displacement, stop reason -- which is what survives the data.

what.description: repo-relative paths removed, as they were named before removal

triggered_by.description: The declared thing that fired. There is deliberately NO free-text reason field: a sentence here would make the trigger a verdict the writer chooses, which is the shape check 6 and check 72 exist to stop, and deletion is its most expensive version because a wrong claim leaves something to read and a deleted trajectory leaves nothing. The reason is the criterion's own `statement` in the plan, by reference -- the same move as `estimation` naming the vocabulary instead of copying it.

kind.description: a stop/success criterion the plan declared before the run, or a named assumption falsifier that fired

declared_in.description: the plan card id and revision that declared it, e.g. plan-sim-20260917-001-r3. The revision is the load-bearing half: an opinion formed after a run has to become a declared criterion in a NEW revision before it can delete anything, and this field is where that shows.

observed_number.description: name of the number that failed it, when the criterion compares one

recorded_in.description:
Repo-relative path of the artifact that records this falsifier firing. Required when `kind` is `falsifier` and refused otherwise.

A falsifier's SENTENCE cannot be recomputed -- it says what would kill an assumption, and whether it happened is usually a fact outside the card, the way a_cost_reference was fired by a wall clock. But the fact is IN THE TREE, so the deletion names where and check 77 resolves the pointer. Without this the two paths to one irreversible act cost differently, and the uncheckable one is the one that gets used -- not from malice but from friction. Architecture ruled it on 2026-09-22, against this seat's own reading that a falsifier is simply not the recomputable kind.
